sections.h2: Where is Hancock County, Kentucky, and what does its layout mean for a home sale?
sections.html:
Hancock County sits on the Ohio River in northwest Kentucky, with Hawesville as the county seat and Lewisport as the largest city. It was formed in 1829 from parts of Breckinridge, Daviess and Ohio counties and is named for John Hancock. The Ohio River forms the northern border across from Indiana, and the county is counted as part of the Owensboro metropolitan area.

The county covers 187.67 square miles of land with roughly 48 residents per square mile, and most of that is rural. The county's industrial foundation describes a riverfront economy built around three aluminum plants and a large paper mill, together with more than 2,000 employees, plus smaller manufacturers and suppliers. The Hancock County school system runs Hancock County High School, Hancock County Middle School, South Hancock Elementary and North Hancock Elementary, which is the only school located in Lewisport.

For a seller, a small market means fewer comparable sales for the assessor and for a buyer's appraiser to use. Census figures count only 15 building permits in 2025, so new construction rarely sets the price for an older house.

sections.h2: Which Hancock County offices handle my property tax bill?
sections.html:
Three offices in the Hancock County Administration Building at 225 Main Cross Street in Hawesville cover almost everything a seller needs. Each one does a separate job, so a call to the wrong desk wastes a day.

  • Sheriff, first floor: collects the bill. Hours run Monday through Friday, 8:00 am to 4:00 pm, at 270-927-6247. Mail goes to P.O. Box 427, Hawesville, KY 42348.
  • Property Valuation Administrator (PVA): assesses all real and personal property. The office does not set rates and does not collect money. Call 270-927-6846 or write to P.O. Box 523.
  • County Clerk, second floor: records land documents and processes delinquent real estate taxes. The number is 270-927-6117, and the mailing address is P.O. Box 146.

The county government's own page points residents to the sheriff for payment, and the PVA's page explains that the Kentucky Department of Revenue supervises the assessor's work each year through county studies.

sections.h2: When are Hancock County property taxes due, and what do late bills cost?
sections.html:
Kentucky sets one calendar for all counties, and the Hancock County Sheriff collects under it. Bills reach the sheriff by September 15, and the PVA says bill preparation usually starts in mid September. The usual schedule under KRS 134.015 looks like this:

  • A 2 percent discount applies when the bill is paid in full by November 1.
  • The face amount is due from November 2 through December 31.
  • A 5 percent penalty applies during January.
  • After January 31 the penalty becomes 10 percent, and the sheriff adds another 10 percent fee.

The Department of Revenue describes the February through April 15 stretch as a 21 percent add-on in total. If bills are mailed late, the state can order an alternative schedule that gives 30 days to each stage. The calendar printed on your own bill controls in that case.

Hancock County bills cover one calendar year, and the tax is a personal debt of whoever owned the property on January 1. Ask the sheriff's office for the exact discount cutoff before you plan a closing in October or November.

sections.h2: What do the Census figures say about Hancock County homes?
sections.html:
Owners hold most of the homes, and values sit well under the Kentucky metro counties. The table below compares what the Census Bureau reports for the county.

More than one in five residents is 65 or older, which matters for taxes: that is the age at which the Kentucky homestead exemption opens up. A $141,200 median home also means the yearly bill is modest in dollars, so a delinquent year or two adds up quickly against the sale price.

sections.h2: How do I dispute a Hancock County assessment?
sections.html:
Start with a conference at the PVA office, because Kentucky does not allow an appeal without one. The tax roll inspection period begins on the first Monday in May and lasts two weeks, ending on the third Monday, and an assessment notice lists the actual dates.

If you and the PVA settle on a number, nothing else is needed. If not, file the appeal with the Hancock County Clerk no later than one workday after inspection closes, and state your own claim of value. A three member local board of assessment appeals hears the case between 25 and 35 days after that. Bring facts, because the board must deny an appeal that arrives without them.

The board sends its decision by certified mail along with instructions for taking the matter to the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals. The Department of Revenue notes that a PVA should be able to hand over the list of sales behind a residential value, so ask for it at the conference.

sections.h2: Does Hancock County offer a homestead exemption for older or disabled owners?
sections.html:
Yes. Owners who are 65 or older, or who are totally disabled, can apply to the Hancock County PVA to reduce the assessed value of the home they live in. The rule is in KRS 132.810.

  • You must own the home and keep it as your personal residence.
  • One exemption is allowed per residential unit, even if two residents qualify.
  • A mobile home or manufactured house counts as a residential unit.
  • The dollar amount moves with a cost of living adjustment every two years, so ask the PVA for the current figure.

Selling ends the exemption for the seller. The statute requires the owner, or an executor or trustee, to report a transfer to the PVA, and the buyer has to apply in their own name if eligible.

sections.h2: What happens to the Hancock County tax bill when I sell the house?
sections.html:
The bill for a given year is issued to whoever owned the property on January 1, so a spring sale still leaves a bill in the seller's name unless the contract says otherwise. The Hancock County PVA mails the current bill to the in care of address written in the deed until bill preparation starts in September, so write a mailing address into the deed that the buyer will actually check.

After the PVA stops handling it, a buyer or seller who never received the bill can ask the sheriff at 270-927-6247 for a copy. The settlement agent normally prorates the year between the parties and pays the sheriff from the closing funds.

Work done before listing may need a permit. Building permits come from the Planning and Zoning office in the old Hancock County Courthouse, which keeps office hours on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays from 8:00 am to noon and answers at 270-927-8169. Unpermitted additions are a common reason a buyer's lender asks questions late in the process.

sections.h2: What happens if a Hancock County bill stays unpaid after April 15?
sections.html:
At the close of business on April 15 the sheriff hands unpaid bills to the County Clerk, where each becomes a certificate of delinquency with a lien recorded against the parcel. Interest runs at 1 percent per month, and the state adds a 10 percent clerk fee and, once the county attorney sends notice, a 20 percent attorney fee.

On the standard calendar the clerk may sell certificates to third party buyers between July 14 and August 28. A buyer who purchases yours can add its own fees on top, so paying before the sale is almost always cheaper. The Hancock County Clerk's website offers a delinquent tax lookup called DTax and a land records viewer, eCCLIX, which is useful for checking a deed chain on an inherited house.

A Hancock County owner with back taxes can still sell. The closing agent asks the clerk or sheriff for a written payoff and settles it from the proceeds, and a cash buyer will usually take the property as it stands with the same payoff step.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in Hancock County, Kentucky?
faqs.a: Pay the Hancock County Sheriff's Office on the first floor of the Administration Building, 225 Main Cross Street, Hawesville, or mail it to P.O. Box 427, Hawesville, KY 42348. Office hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 am to 4:00 pm, and the phone is 270-927-6247.

faqs.q: Who sets my home's assessed value in Hancock County?
faqs.a: The Property Valuation Administrator does. The PVA values property at fair cash value as of January 1 and does not set tax rates or collect payments. Call 270-927-6846 with questions about value.

faqs.q: Will a house I sell in spring still produce a tax bill in my name?
faqs.a: Yes, usually. Kentucky issues the bill to the January 1 owner, so the seller is the named taxpayer for that year. The contract and the settlement statement decide who ultimately pays each share.

faqs.q: How can I check whether a Hancock County parcel has delinquent taxes?
faqs.a: Use the delinquent tax lookup on the Hancock County Clerk's website, or call the clerk at 270-927-6117. The site says the amounts shown are informational and that the clerk decides the actual dollar figure at the time of payment or sale.

faqs.q: Where do I get a building permit in Hancock County?
faqs.a: Go to the Planning and Zoning office in the old Hancock County Courthouse in Hawesville, open Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays from 8:00 am to noon. The office number is 270-927-8169.
